cards.q: Describe an astronomical refracting telescope in normal adjustment.
cards.a: Two converging lenses: an objective of long focal length and an eyepiece of short focal length, separated by the sum of their focal lengths. The final image is at infinity.
cards.why: The objective forms a real image at its focal point, which is also the focal point of the eyepiece.

cards.q: Define the angular magnification of a telescope in normal adjustment.
cards.a: M=angle subtended by the image at the eyeangle subtended by the object at the unaided eye\displaystyle M = \frac{\text{angle subtended by the image at the eye}}{\text{angle subtended by the object at the unaided eye}}M=angle subtended by the object at the unaided eyeangle subtended by the image at the eye​

cards.q: A refracting telescope has an objective of focal length 1.2 m and an eyepiece of focal length 0.040 m. Calculate its angular magnification in normal adjustment.
cards.a: 30
steps: M=fofe=1.20.040\displaystyle M = \frac{f_{o}}{f_{e}} = \frac{1.2}{0.040}M=fe​fo​​=0.0401.2​
M=30\displaystyle M = 30M=30

cards.q: Describe the Cassegrain arrangement of a reflecting telescope.
cards.a: A large concave parabolic primary mirror reflects light on to a small convex secondary mirror, which reflects it back through a hole in the centre of the primary to the eyepiece.

cards.q: What is chromatic aberration, and which kind of telescope suffers from it?
cards.a: A lens refracts different wavelengths by different amounts, so different colours focus at different points and the image has coloured edges. It affects refracting telescopes; mirrors do not cause it.

cards.q: What is spherical aberration, and how is it avoided in a reflecting telescope?
cards.a: Rays striking the outer part of a spherical mirror or lens are brought to a focus at a different point from rays near the centre, blurring the image. It is avoided by using a parabolic mirror.

cards.q: Give three advantages of reflecting telescopes over refracting telescopes.
cards.a: No chromatic aberration, large mirrors are practical, and less light is lost.
marks: Mirrors do not cause chromatic aberration.
A large mirror can be supported from behind, so it can be made much bigger than a lens, which sags under its own weight.
Light does not pass through glass, so less is absorbed, and a parabolic mirror removes spherical aberration.

cards.q: Give one similarity and two differences between a single-dish radio telescope and an optical reflecting telescope.
cards.a: Similarity: both use a parabolic dish or mirror to bring radiation to a focus. Differences: radio waves have much longer wavelengths, so a radio telescope has a much poorer resolving power for the same diameter; and its dish can be a wire mesh, because it need not be as smooth.

cards.q: Why are ultraviolet and X-ray telescopes placed in orbit, while radio telescopes work on the ground?
cards.a: The atmosphere absorbs ultraviolet and X-rays, so they must be observed from above it. The atmosphere is transparent to radio waves.
cards.why: Infrared is absorbed mainly by water vapour, so infrared telescopes are in orbit or on high, dry mountains.

cards.q: State the Rayleigh criterion for the minimum angular resolution of a telescope.
cards.a: θ≈λD\displaystyle \theta \approx \frac{\lambda}{D}θ≈Dλ​, where θ\displaystyle \thetaθ is the smallest angular separation that can be resolved (in radians), λ\displaystyle \lambdaλ the wavelength and D\displaystyle DD the diameter of the aperture.
cards.why: A smaller θ\displaystyle \thetaθ is better: a larger diameter or a shorter wavelength resolves finer detail.

cards.q: Calculate the minimum angular resolution of a telescope of diameter 2.4 m observing light of wavelength 550 nm.
cards.a: 2.3×10−7 rad\displaystyle 2.3 \times 10^{-7}\ \text{rad}2.3×10−7 rad
steps: θ≈λD=550×10−92.4\displaystyle \theta \approx \frac{\lambda}{D} = \frac{550 \times 10^{-9}}{2.4}θ≈Dλ​=2.4550×10−9​
θ=2.3×10−7 rad\displaystyle \theta = 2.3 \times 10^{-7}\ \text{rad}θ=2.3×10−7 rad

cards.q: The diameter of a telescope is doubled. How does its collecting power change?
cards.a: It becomes four times as great: collecting power is proportional to the diameter squared.

cards.q: Compare a CCD with the eye as a detector, in terms of quantum efficiency and convenience.
cards.a: A CCD has a much higher quantum efficiency (about 80%, against about 1% for the eye), so it detects far fainter objects. It can also be exposed for a long time, records the image for analysis, and detects wavelengths the eye cannot.
cards.why: Quantum efficiency is the percentage of incident photons that are detected.

cards.q: What is the apparent magnitude of a star?
cards.a: A measure of how bright the star appears from Earth. The scale runs backwards: the brighter the star, the lower the number. The dimmest stars visible to the naked eye have a magnitude of about 6.

cards.q: What intensity ratio corresponds to a difference of 1 in apparent magnitude?
cards.a: A ratio of 2.51. A difference of 5 magnitudes is a ratio of 100.

cards.q: Star A has an apparent magnitude of 1 and star B has an apparent magnitude of 4. How many times brighter does A appear than B?
cards.a: About 16 times
cards.why: The lower magnitude is the brighter star.
steps: The magnitudes differ by 3.
Each magnitude is a factor of 2.51: 2.513\displaystyle 2.51^{3}2.513
=16\displaystyle = 16=16

cards.q: Define the absolute magnitude of a star.
cards.a: The apparent magnitude the star would have at a distance of 10 parsecs from the observer.
cards.why: It compares the true brightness of stars, with the effect of distance removed.

cards.q: A star has an apparent magnitude of 7.0 and is 100 pc away. Calculate its absolute magnitude.
cards.a: 2.0
steps: m−M=5log⁡(d10)\displaystyle m - M = 5\log\left(\frac{d}{10}\right)m−M=5log(10d​), with d\displaystyle dd in parsecs.
7.0−M=5log⁡(10010)=5×1=5\displaystyle 7.0 - M = 5\log\left(\frac{100}{10}\right) = 5 \times 1 = 57.0−M=5log(10100​)=5×1=5
M=2.0\displaystyle M = 2.0M=2.0

cards.q: Define the parsec and the light year.
cards.a: Parsec: the distance at which the radius of the Earth's orbit (1 AU) subtends an angle of one second of arc. Light year: the distance light travels in a vacuum in one year.

cards.q: Explain how trigonometric parallax is used to find the distance to a nearby star.
cards.a: The star's apparent shift against distant stars is measured from opposite sides of the Earth's orbit.
marks: Observe the star's position against the background of very distant stars.
Observe it again six months later, when the Earth is on the opposite side of its orbit.
Half the angle the star has appeared to shift is the parallax angle.
With the radius of the Earth's orbit as a known baseline, trigonometry gives the distance: the smaller the angle, the more distant the star.

cards.q: Write the equation for the intensity of radiation at a distance d\displaystyle dd from a star of luminosity L\displaystyle LL. What does it assume?
cards.a: I=L4πd2\displaystyle I = \frac{L}{4\pi d^{2}}I=4πd2L​. It assumes the star radiates equally in all directions and that none of the radiation is absorbed on the way.
cards.why: Luminosity is the total power the star radiates.

cards.q: The Sun has a luminosity of 3.85×1026 W\displaystyle 3.85 \times 10^{26}\ \text{W}3.85×1026 W and is 1.50×1011 m\displaystyle 1.50 \times 10^{11}\ \text{m}1.50×1011 m from the Earth. Calculate the intensity of its radiation at the Earth.
cards.a: 1.4×103 W m−2\displaystyle 1.4 \times 10^{3}\ \text{W m}^{-2}1.4×103 W m−2
steps: I=L4πd2=3.85×10264π(1.50×1011)2\displaystyle I = \frac{L}{4\pi d^{2}} = \frac{3.85 \times 10^{26}}{4\pi (1.50 \times 10^{11})^{2}}I=4πd2L​=4π(1.50×1011)23.85×1026​
I=1.4×103 W m−2\displaystyle I = 1.4 \times 10^{3}\ \text{W m}^{-2}I=1.4×103 W m−2

cards.q: What is a standard candle, and how is it used to find a distance?
cards.a: An object of known luminosity. Measuring the intensity received on Earth and using I=L4πd2\displaystyle I = \frac{L}{4\pi d^{2}}I=4πd2L​ gives its distance.

cards.q: What is a black body?
cards.a: An object that absorbs all the radiation falling on it, and emits a continuous spectrum that depends only on its temperature. Stars are treated as black bodies.

cards.q: Describe how a black-body radiation curve (intensity against wavelength) changes as the temperature rises.
cards.a: The peak gets higher and moves to a shorter wavelength, and the area under the curve (the total power) increases greatly.

cards.q: State Wien's displacement law.
cards.a: The wavelength at which a black body emits most strongly is inversely proportional to its absolute temperature: λmaxT=2.9×10−3 m K\displaystyle \lambda_{\text{max}}T = 2.9 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{m K}λmax​T=2.9×10−3 m K.

cards.q: A star's spectrum peaks at a wavelength of 500 nm. Estimate its surface temperature. (λmaxT=2.9×10−3 m K\displaystyle \lambda_{\text{max}}T = 2.9 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{m K}λmax​T=2.9×10−3 m K)
cards.a: 5800 K
steps: T=2.9×10−3λmax=2.9×10−3500×10−9\displaystyle T = \frac{2.9 \times 10^{-3}}{\lambda_{\text{max}}} = \frac{2.9 \times 10^{-3}}{500 \times 10^{-9}}T=λmax​2.9×10−3​=500×10−92.9×10−3​
T=5800 K\displaystyle T = 5800\ \text{K}T=5800 K

cards.q: State Stefan's law for the power radiated by a black body.
cards.a: P=σAT4\displaystyle P = \sigma AT^{4}P=σAT4: the power is proportional to the surface area and to the fourth power of the absolute temperature.

edexcel.note: Edexcel writes this as L=σAT4\displaystyle L = \sigma AT^{4}L=σAT4, with L\displaystyle LL the luminosity.

cards.q: The Sun has a radius of 6.96×108 m\displaystyle 6.96 \times 10^{8}\ \text{m}6.96×108 m and a surface temperature of 5800 K. Calculate the power it radiates. (σ=5.67×10−8 W m−2 K−4\displaystyle \sigma = 5.67 \times 10^{-8}\ \text{W m}^{-2}\ \text{K}^{-4}σ=5.67×10−8 W m−2 K−4)
cards.a: 3.9×1026 W\displaystyle 3.9 \times 10^{26}\ \text{W}3.9×1026 W
steps: Surface area of a sphere: A=4πr2=4π(6.96×108)2=6.09×1018 m2\displaystyle A = 4\pi r^{2} = 4\pi (6.96 \times 10^{8})^{2} = 6.09 \times 10^{18}\ \text{m}^{2}A=4πr2=4π(6.96×108)2=6.09×1018 m2.
P=σAT4=5.67×10−8×6.09×1018×58004\displaystyle P = \sigma AT^{4} = 5.67 \times 10^{-8} \times 6.09 \times 10^{18} \times 5800^{4}P=σAT4=5.67×10−8×6.09×1018×58004
P=3.9×1026 W\displaystyle P = 3.9 \times 10^{26}\ \text{W}P=3.9×1026 W

cards.q: Two stars have the same radius. One has twice the surface temperature of the other. How do their power outputs compare?
cards.a: The hotter star radiates 16 times as much power.
cards.why: P∝T4\displaystyle P \propto T^{4}P∝T4, and 24=16\displaystyle 2^{4} = 1624=16.

cards.q: List the seven spectral classes of stars in order from hottest to coolest, and give the colours of the hottest and coolest.
cards.a: O B A F G K M. Class O stars are blue; class M stars are red.
cards.why: The Sun is class G: yellow-white, about 5800 K.

cards.q: Explain why hydrogen Balmer absorption lines are strongest in class A stars, and weak in much hotter and much cooler stars.
cards.a: The lines need hydrogen atoms with electrons in the n=2\displaystyle n = 2n=2 state.
marks: Balmer lines are produced when electrons in the n=2\displaystyle n = 2n=2 level absorb photons.
In cool stars almost all hydrogen atoms are in the ground state, so few can absorb these wavelengths.
In very hot stars most hydrogen is ionised, so there are few electrons in n=2\displaystyle n = 2n=2.
At the temperature of class A stars the largest proportion of hydrogen atoms is in the n=2\displaystyle n = 2n=2 state.

cards.q: Describe the axes of a Hertzsprung–Russell diagram and the positions of its three main groups of stars.
cards.a: Luminosity (or absolute magnitude) is plotted against surface temperature, with temperature decreasing to the right. The main sequence is a diagonal band from top left to bottom right; giants are at the top right; white dwarfs are at the bottom left.

cards.a: It leaves the main sequence and moves up and to the right, becoming a red giant: cooler but far more luminous. It then moves across and down to the bottom left, ending as a white dwarf: hot but dim.

cards.q: A red giant is cooler than the Sun but far more luminous. How is this possible?
cards.a: Its surface area is enormously larger. P=σAT4\displaystyle P = \sigma AT^{4}P=σAT4: the huge area more than makes up for the lower temperature.
cards.why: A white dwarf is the reverse: hot, but so small that its luminosity is low.

cards.q: State the defining property of a supernova, of a neutron star and of a black hole.
cards.a: Supernova: a rapid, enormous increase in brightness (absolute magnitude). Neutron star: made almost entirely of neutrons, with the density of nuclear matter. Black hole: its escape velocity is greater than the speed of light.

cards.why: This is the radius of the event horizon: nothing inside it, not even light, can escape.

cards.q: Why can type 1a supernovae be used as standard candles?
cards.a: They all reach about the same peak absolute magnitude, so their luminosity is known. Comparing this with how bright one appears gives its distance.

cards.q: Describe the light curve of a typical type 1a supernova.
cards.a: A rapid rise to a sharp peak in brightness over about 20 days, followed by a slower, gradual decline over many months.

cards.q: What did observations of distant type 1a supernovae suggest about the expansion of the Universe?
cards.a: The supernovae were dimmer, and so further away, than expected. This suggests the expansion of the Universe is accelerating, which has been attributed to dark energy. Its nature is not understood, and the idea remains controversial.

cards.q: What causes a gamma ray burst, and how does its energy output compare with the Sun's?
cards.a: The collapse of a supergiant star to form a neutron star or a black hole. In a few seconds it can release as much energy as the Sun emits in its entire lifetime.

cards.q: Where are supermassive black holes found?
cards.a: At the centres of galaxies.

cards.q: What is the Doppler effect?
cards.a: The change in the observed frequency (and wavelength) of a wave when the source and the observer are moving relative to each other.

cards.q: Write the equations for the red shift z\displaystyle zz of light from a source moving at speed v\displaystyle vv, much less than the speed of light.
cards.a: z=Δλλ=Δff=vc\displaystyle z = \frac{\Delta\lambda}{\lambda} = \frac{\Delta f}{f} = \frac{v}{c}z=λΔλ​=fΔf​=cv​ in magnitude.
cards.why: A source moving away gives a longer wavelength (red shift); one approaching gives a shorter wavelength (blue shift).

cards.q: A hydrogen line of wavelength 656.3 nm in the laboratory is observed at 662.9 nm in the light from a galaxy. Calculate the speed of the galaxy relative to the Earth. (c=3.00×108 m s−1\displaystyle c = 3.00 \times 10^{8}\ \text{m s}^{-1}c=3.00×108 m s−1)
cards.a: 3.0×106 m s−1\displaystyle 3.0 \times 10^{6}\ \text{m s}^{-1}3.0×106 m s−1, moving away.
cards.why: The wavelength has increased, so the galaxy is receding.

cards.q: A binary star system is viewed in the plane of its orbit. Explain how its spectrum shows that it is two stars.
cards.a: Each spectral line splits in two and merges again as the stars orbit.
marks: When one star moves towards the Earth and the other away, their lines are blue-shifted and red-shifted, so each line appears split.
When both stars move across the line of sight there is no shift along it, and the lines coincide.
The pattern repeats with the period of the orbit.
The greatest shift gives the orbital speed of the stars.

cards.q: State Hubble's law.
cards.a: The speed at which a distant galaxy is receding is directly proportional to its distance: v=H0d\displaystyle v = H_{0}dv=H0​d.

cards.q: Take the Hubble constant as 70 km s−1 Mpc−1\displaystyle 70\ \text{km s}^{-1}\ \text{Mpc}^{-1}70 km s−1 Mpc−1. Calculate the recession speed of a galaxy 50 Mpc away.
cards.a: 3.5×103 km s−1\displaystyle 3.5 \times 10^{3}\ \text{km s}^{-1}3.5×103 km s−1
cards.why: With the constant in these units, the distance stays in megaparsecs and the speed comes out in kilometres per second.

cards.q: Estimate the age of the Universe, taking the Hubble constant as 2.2×10−18 s−1\displaystyle 2.2 \times 10^{-18}\ \text{s}^{-1}2.2×10−18 s−1 and assuming it has stayed constant.
cards.a: 4.5×1017 s\displaystyle 4.5 \times 10^{17}\ \text{s}4.5×1017 s (about 14 billion years)

cards.q: How is Hubble's law interpreted?
cards.a: The Universe is expanding: space itself is stretching, so every galaxy is moving away from every other, and the further apart they are the faster they separate.

cards.q: Give two pieces of evidence for the Big Bang theory, other than the red shift of galaxies.
cards.a: The cosmic microwave background radiation: radiation from the hot early Universe, now stretched to microwave wavelengths and coming from every direction. And the relative abundance of hydrogen and helium, which matches what fusion in the first few minutes would have produced.

cards.q: Explain why there is uncertainty about the age and the ultimate fate of the Universe.
cards.a: Both depend on quantities that are hard to measure: the Hubble constant and the amount of matter.
marks: The age is estimated from 1H0\displaystyle \frac{1}{H_{0}}H0​1​, and the Hubble constant is uncertain because distances to far galaxies are hard to measure.
The fate of the Universe depends on its average density: enough matter and gravity could halt the expansion.
Much of the matter appears to be dark matter, which does not emit light and is detected only through its gravity, so the total mass is uncertain.

cards.q: What are quasars, and how were they first discovered?
cards.a: Extremely luminous objects with very large red shifts: the most distant measurable objects. They were first found as bright sources of radio waves. They are thought to be active supermassive black holes at the centres of young galaxies.

cards.q: Why is it difficult to detect an exoplanet directly?
cards.a: The planet is very close to its star, so the angle between them is tiny, and the star is enormously brighter, so its light swamps the faint light reflected by the planet.

cards.q: Explain how the radial velocity method detects an exoplanet.
cards.a: The planet makes its star wobble, which shows as a regular Doppler shift.
marks: The star and the planet orbit their common centre of mass, so the star moves in a small orbit.
The star moves alternately towards and away from the Earth.
Its spectral lines are alternately blue-shifted and red-shifted.
A regular, repeating shift shows that a planet is present, and its period is the planet's orbital period.

cards.q: Describe how the transit method detects an exoplanet, and the light curve it produces.
cards.a: When the planet passes in front of its star it blocks a little of the light. The light curve shows a small, flat-bottomed dip in brightness that repeats each time the planet completes an orbit.
